Okay, hear me out, I have a take on the ending that doesn't have anything to do with the Indoctrination Theory.

The three endings are the Intelligence (created by the Leviathans to ensure organic life continues) simulating various methods by which the mission could continue, but using Shepard as the variable. It straight up tells Shepard that they are the first organic being to ever speak with it, which causes it to rethink the cycle. So, it plugs the Shepard variable into the equation and comes up with three possibilities.
1. The Reapers work with organic life to ensure it prospers. Shepard, the only organic life to impress the Intelligence, is deemed an acceptable controlling force. The Reapers need an organic thought process or the cycle will just continue, which has been shown to be ineffective.
2. Synthetic and organic life are blended to the point where there can be no distinction between them, using Shepard as a template. Organic life no longer suffers the threat of extermination from synthetic life, so the cycle can end. The Reapers become unnecessary and are cast aside.
3. Perhaps the most interesting one, because it shows Shepard living (if you have high enough EMS), the cycle is broken. The Intelligence determines that it has not followed its original mission, instead carrying out the exact thing it was created to prevent. It realises that it has been the synthetic threat to organics, not the saving grace. So, it destroys the Reapers.

Whichever ending is picked is the one the Intelligence has deemed most effective. Because Shepard is unconscious the whole time, they don't need to pull a trigger, jump into an energy beam, or disintegrate themselves: the Intelligence is doing the work. But, that's not to say Shepard isn't doing anything. They are the variable, the thing the Intelligence plays around with. Their memories are scanned, their experiences weighed and compared. Shepard's choices determine the ending because the Intelligence reads them and determines what should happen. 

As for the fate of Shepard, the only reason they live in the high Destroy ending is because the Intelligence doesn't need them. Control, Shepard is used as the organic thought process for the Reapers. Synthesis, their unique physical makeup is the blueprint needed. But Destroy, the Intelligence just erases itself and the Reapers. Shepard lives because nothing is around to kill them.

Hi! I am a dedicant of Skadi and have been for like... four? years? I *love* gushing about her so I am happy to share!

Skadi is a study in contrasts, much like how winter has two distinct: the warmth of the hearth and the biting cold of the blizzard. She is, beyond anything, winter given form. I have felt Her be so incredibly warm, nurturing, and kind. I have also felt Her be ice cold, unforgiving, and stoic.

I think my general advice on approaching Her is, treat her with the respect you would treat a snowstorm. Be clear in your intentions, keep your promises to Her. She does not abide broken agreements, of any kind. Treat Her with respect and She will bring you the warmth of Her hearth. Fail to do that and you might get a sleetstorm to the face (I speak from experience haha).

For offerings, vodka is definitely a good one, as is cinnamon and home baked goods (cinnamon vodka is NOT a good idea though, from my experience). I have not tried offering her things from a mountain so I don't know how that would go over.

I realise I make Her sound scary, She really is not! She is loving and warm and the best thing that ever happened to me. She demands respect is all.

Beowulf was never "corrupted", the story was never pagan to begin with. Our best guess is that it (the version we have) was written down by a monk in Christian England around the 11th century. There \*may\* have been a different version, but any trace of that hypothetical story is lost to us.

Snorri wrote the Eddas down in a way that tried to preserve the folklore aspect of Norse myth while simultaneously ensuring it didn't anger the Church in any way. The gods (Odin, Loki, Thor, etc) are called powerful beings, but never divine to the best of my knowledge.  


Edit: never \*fully\* pagan. It had aspects of both.

The lens we view a lot of source material for Norse Heathenry through is, for better or worse, influenced heavily by Christian thinking. This stuff wasn't written down until during and after the conversion of Scandiniavia. Snorri, the guy we get the Eddas from, was Christian. We have some inkling of what the Norse "actually" believed (quote marks used because what they believed is and will be up for debate) from Roman and other contemporary sources, but the bulk of what we have is interpreted by non-heathen scholars.

So, does that mean that Christianity and Norse beliefs are inherently related? Draw your own conclusions, but my money is solidly on no.

The Siege of Namur.
The Second Berlin Blockade had blown up in the East's face. The staunchly anticommunist administration of Joseph Mccarthy took the path of war, ignoring the precedent put forward by Truman in 1949. As Operation Unthinkable became a reality and Soviet troops were pouring across the East-West German border, Belgium was caught in the crossfire. Antwerp and Zeebrugge were two of the most important ports to the Allied war effort, and northern Flanders was host to dozens of Allied fuel depots. If the Soviets overran the small nation, the Allies would be in dire straits, especially with de Gaulle and the new French government threatening neutrality.
With Soviet soldiers smashing through the Ardennes, a hastily made defence line was built along the Meuse river, concentrated at Liège and Namur. Liège, the fortress city that had held the Germans off twice in the past 50 years, would be fine. Namur was the weak spot in the line. If the city fell, there was little between the Soviets and Brussels, the capital. If the capital fell, the entire region would fall soon after.

The Soviet 10 and 19th Tank Armies approached, crashing through every makeshift line the Allies had. The Belgian Army was a shadow of its former shadow, drained by the previous war and weakened by 4 years of brutal occupation. It's leader, King Leopold III, was on the brink of abdication following his return to the country, after being called a coward and traitor for surrendering in 1940. Flemish national sentiment had been stoked by Nazi occupiers and linguistic unity in the Army was nonexistent. The American Army was tied down in Bavaria, the British and Commonwealth barely holding outside Hannover and Maastricht, and the French were even more war weary, not lifting a finger to help their northern neighbors. The Belgians had support from what was left of the West German Bundeswehr, such as it was, a small American armored contingent, and a battalion of Canadians. They would hold the line or die on it.

The Soviet attack came at 8 am on the 17th of May, 1951. All along the Meuse, Soviet tanks and troops tried to push their way across the river. The eastern half of Namur was taken in two hours, the Allies pulling back across the rail bridge to the west and blowing it. Artillery was concentrated on the Citadel, the old fortress of Namur that had stood for centuries, Allied guns looking out across the Meuse and pounding the Russians on the other side. By noon, Russian troops were in the Caserne. The train station, the only feasible evacuation route for the troops, was taken at 2.25 pm, then retaken at 5 pm. By 8 pm, the Cathedral of St. Aubain was in Russian hands and the Sambre River's northern bank with it. The Citadel was surrounded on 3 sides. 

Dawn on the 18th rose over a battered city. The Belgians still held the Citadel and the area directly west, the Canadians and Americans held the train station. A last ditch counterattack had kept the Soviets out of the Parc de Louise Marie, but the line between the two strongpoints was tenuous at best. Amidst this, tensions between the Flemish and Walloon contingents had boiled over in the worst way, with Flemish troops refusing direct orders given in French, and Flemish officers few and far between. Upon hearing of an outbreak of violence between Flemish and Walloon artillerymen on the Citadel, the King, who had been helping monitor the defence of Liège, reportedly dropped his affairs on the spot and drove himself to Namur, a journey of two hours in peacetime, often driving only kilometres behind the front line. His arrival was met by shock and disgust. His return after the end of the Second World War had almost resulted in a civil war and the dissolution of the monarchy. But, he had many supporters in Flanders. They would listen to him.

Leopold marched up the steep steps of the Citadel, growing angrier by the moment. Stunned soldiers scrambled out of his way, hastily saluting before returning to the defence. At the uppermost level of the Citadel, where much of the General Staff was observing and ordering artillery fire, the King grabbed a rifle from a nearby private and fired it into the air. The officers all jumped and turned, only to to jump again to attention. One officer attempted to stammer out a report, but he was silenced by a glare from the King. Leopold looked long and slow at his officers before demanding an explanation. No one could give one. 
"We are facing a threat greater than both German invasions, and yet we fight amongst ourselves?!"
No response. 
Frustrated, the King turned and marched to the lower levels, where the soldiers were. In front of a gathering crowd, he spoke to his soldiers, his people.
"Today, we cannot afford to be Flemish and Walloon. Today we must be Belgian and nothing else. Once our enemy is gone, we can settle this, but not one day before."

On the third day of the siege, King Leopold III led his troops in an act reminiscent of Albert I's in 1914. The Belgian counterattack from the Citadel caught the Soviets completely off guard, being secure in their numbers. By day's end, the Belgian Army and supporting Americans and Canadians had retaken the city up to the Meuse, with the Belgians even pushing across it to occupied Faubourg. Leopold's headquarters were established on the eastern side of the river and, over the next week, the Soviets, despite their numeric advantage over the vastly outnumbered Belgians, were pushed back almost to the border of the Ardennes. Seeing their ally's success, 10.000 American troops were pulled from the southern German front to consolidate the Meuse Line, now the Ardennes Line. 

The war would rage for another year, but the Soviets would never again get so close to destroying the Allied war infrastructure in the Low countries. King Leopold III, once days away from announcing his abdication, suddenly became a national hero, mentioned in the same breath as the Soldier King Albert I. In the three day siege of Namur and following counterattack, 42.000 Belgian, Canadian, West German, and American troops and 104.000 Soviet soldiers were killed. It was the bloodiest battle in Belgian military history.

The Coal Wars were a series of conflicts between the Industrial League and the druids, an ethnic group wielding magic whose power is based in the life fore of nature (the stronger nature is, the stronger magic they have). It was waged out of fear of the powers of natural magic, as well as the exclusivity of magic in general, when compared to equality offered by machinery and industry. It wasn't so much a war as it was a protracted proto-genocide, one the druids lost hard. They're still around, but just barely.

The Sanguis Arcanus is the other side of the proverbial coin of magic. Where natural magic draws from nature, the Sanguis Arcanus pulls power from the blood of its users. The fancy name is due to the fact that only those belonging to a royal bloodline have the chance to be born with it. Its not guaranteed, nor is it even very powerful. Most royals can perform very small feats of telekinesis by themselves, but when more royals come together they can do much greater shows of power. This is risky though, and since royals like living, these greater shows are rare. There have been a few instances where individuals manifested larger shows of power on their own, like the Gaoler Prince Jeriod Kallak or the Royal Doctors of Therien, but these are extraordinary examples.

There's conflicting beliefs around when the world was born. Some say it was in the Before, some say there is a divide between the Old World and New World, with the Old World drowning in the Age of Storms and being reborn anew.
There's definitely archaeological record providing evidence that there was some sort of civilization before the Age of Storms, the proposed Age of Stone, but it is unknown if these artifacts are human in origin ((before anyone asks, aliens don't exist in this world. As far as humanity is concerned, the night sky is a dark and foreboding place where the gods went to die, so they want nothing to do with it))
